10.body: The essay blends two distinct voices, kept separate throughout these pages: Dr. Robert K. Naviaux's framework & published research: Terminology such as the Cell Danger Response , Healing Cycle (CDR1–CDR3), Health Cycle , salugenesis , metabolomic/hypometabolic findings in ME/CFS and long-COVID, and low-dose suramin pilot research in autism spectrum disorder. A Midwestern Doctor's clinical commentary & hypotheses: Observations from integrative/regenerative practice, commentary on pharmaceuticals, vaccines, spike protein injuries, surgical anesthetics, reverse T3 / low-dose T3, zeta potential, DMSO, and institutional critiques. These pages are study notes summarizing a public essay , not medical advice or peer-reviewed clinical guidelines. 11.body: In his work on the Cell Danger Response, Dr. Robert K. Naviaux draws a sharp distinction between the Healing Cycle (temporary cellular defense and repair triggered by injury or threat) and the Health Cycle (the daily physiological state that builds resilience and prevents chronic defense states from locking in). To enter and sustain the Health Cycle, Naviaux identifies six core inputs—a process he calls salugenesis (actively generating health rather than merely fighting pathology): "The six cardinal elements of the health cycle are 1) wakeful activity, 2) nutrient intake, 3) waste and toxin removal, 4) social connection [and positive social support], 5) nature connection, and 6) restorative sleep. Absence of, or abnormalities in, any of the cardinal elements of the health cycle can lead to pluricausal disease [while] their presence contributes to the building of functional reserve capacity and resilient health over the weeks and months after injury or illness." — Dr. Robert K. Naviaux , quoted in Systemic Treatments for the Cell Danger Response

11.title: The Health Cycle & Six Cardinal Elements

12.body: Element Role in the Health Cycle What Happens When Missing or Disrupted 1. Wakeful activity Signals purposeful demand, metabolic turnover, and physical movement without crossing into exhaustion Deconditioning on one extreme, or post-exertional "crashes" when pushed past tolerance 2. Nutrient intake Supplies cellular building blocks for tissue rebuilding (CDR2) and normal differentiation (CDR3) Cells lack substrates to repair and re-enter energy-producing metabolism 3. Waste & toxin removal Clears chemical stressors, cellular debris, and metabolic byproducts so danger alarms quiet down Sub-toxic accumulation compounds past the body's tipping point and re-triggers the CDR 4. Social connection Provides positive social support that feeds safety and security signaling through the brain and nervous system Isolation or threat reinforces sympathetic fight-or-flight tone and danger signaling 5. Nature connection Aligns the body with natural environmental cues (light/dark, temperature, unhurried rhythms) Modern artificial environments desynchronize circadian and autonomic regulation 6. Restorative sleep Delivers deep delta-wave sleep and parasympathetic nervous system safety signals across the body Fragmented sleep or sedative-suppressed sleep prevents systemic termination of the CDR

13.body: Naviaux's framing resolves two common puzzles in chronic illness: Pluricausal disease: Chronic conditions rarely stem from a single broken part. Deficits across several of the six elements lower the threshold at which an infection, toxin, trauma, or emotional shock tips cells into a sustained Cell Danger Response . Functional reserve capacity: Cultivating all six elements doesn't act like an overnight drug—it gradually rebuilds reserve capacity over weeks and months following injury or illness.

14.body: According to clinical observations shared in the essay, stabilizing a newly recovered baseline takes roughly three months ("the length of a season") . During that fragile post-recovery window, an abrupt return of stressors—or even over-eager therapies—can easily re-trigger the CDR pattern before the Health Cycle has consolidated. 15.body: Reflecting on Naviaux's Six Cardinal Elements , A Midwestern Doctor highlights a foundational blind spot in modern healthcare: medicine is organized around naming and suppressing diseases rather than cultivating the underlying generators of health. "Medicine typically focuses on identifying and 'treating' diseases rather than identifying what creates health and cultivating that. Although the disease-focused model can often seem very impressive (and generate a lot of business from each identified 'disease'), without cultivating the core generators of health, complex chronic diseases will continually arise that cannot be fixed within the disease-centered model." — A Midwestern Doctor , Systemic Treatments for the Cell Danger Response

18.body: Because the CDR activates once a person's cumulative burden (sub-toxic chemicals, infections, trauma, disrupted sleep/rhythms) crosses a threshold, two patients with identical diagnoses (e.g., ME/CFS, long-COVID, autoimmunity) may have arrived via completely different trigger histories. Conversely, the same environmental stressor can produce different symptoms depending on which tissue remained trapped in the CDR.

19.body: When a condition spans hormones, nerves, immunity, fatigue, and mood simultaneously, single-cause diagnostics come back inconclusive. As the essay notes, sufferers are frequently dismissed as having "psychosomatic" illness—made worse by a two-way biological loop: An active CDR frequently generates neuroinflammation, depression, and anxiety directly. Negative emotions and perceived danger signal the brain to reinforce the CDR, blocking the calm safety signals needed to exit it.

22.body: The Cell Danger Response (CDR) is a conserved cellular defense program initiated by mitochondria when they detect chemical, microbial, physical, or energetic danger. Rather than viewing mitochondria solely as static "powerhouses" that malfunction randomly, Naviaux's framework sees them as danger sensors that intentionally switch from normal energy-and-work mode into cellular defense mode.
22.breadcrumbs: What Is the Cell Danger Response (CDR)? » What Is the Cell Danger Response (CDR)?
22.title: What Is the Cell Danger Response (CDR)?

23.body: Resource diversion: Mitochondria shift cellular resources away from specialized organ tasks toward a low-functioning defensive state designed to contain pathogens (such as viruses) and survive toxic stress. Neighbor warning: Triggered cells release danger signals (notably extracellular ATP) warning neighboring cells to enter the CDR as well. Disconnection from the organism: While in survival mode, cells prioritize individual preservation over tissue cooperation and become partially deaf to external signals: Hormone resistance: Cells reduce responsiveness to hormones such as thyroid hormone and insulin. Autonomic nerve disconnection: Altered responsiveness to nervous-system signaling shows up in autonomic metrics such as heart rate and heart rate variability (HRV) .
23.breadcrumbs: What Is the Cell Danger Response (CDR)? » What Happens When a Cell Enters the CDR
23.title: What Happens When a Cell Enters the CDR

24.body: Healthy Completion ("The Healing Cycle") Trapped Activation (Chronic Illness) Trigger → CDR1 → CDR2 → CDR3 → Safety signals → normal function Something blocks completion or danger persists Damaged components are cleared, repaired, and upgraded Endless cycle of cellular hypofunction, inflammation, or proliferation Underlying protection that makes recovery from injury possible Presents clinically as "mitochondrial dysfunction" and complex multi-system disease Because the CDR is inherently a healing program when allowed to finish, Dr. Robert K. Naviaux later renamed its normal arc the Healing Cycle .

25.body: The essay highlights why chronic CDR activation appears more common today: modern environments expose people to vast mixtures of synthetic chemicals—each individually below classic "toxic" thresholds—alongside infections, trauma, and disrupted biological rhythms . When total stressors exceed a tipping point, the CDR flips into a chronic, self-sustaining loop expressing symptoms tied to whichever tissues are trapped.

26.body: A Midwestern Doctor notes that patterns seen in long-COVID and spike-protein injuries closely match earlier complex chronic CDR cases. Citing Dr. Robert K. Naviaux's metabolomic research : Not a broken engine, but an altered survival state: Metabolomic profiling indicates that patients with long-COVID (PASC) and ME/CFS do not have random, generalized mitochondrial damage—they have entered a specific hypometabolic survival state . Why post-exertional malaise ("crashes") happens: Physical or emotional exertion triggers autonomic and neuroendocrine activation that temporarily forces cells backward from a later repair phase ( Phase 3A ) back into glycolytic metabolism and inflammation ( Phase 1C ). Downstream cascade: Naviaux links this state to mitochondrial hyperfusion, hypersensitivity to ATP signaling, innate immunity shifts, neutrophil and NK-cell dysfunction, neurologic symptoms, latent DNA virus and endogenous retrovirus reactivation, misfolded protein aggregates, and increased vulnerability to apoptosis and ferroptosis. Exit signal: Restoring long-distance brain-body signaling at the end of Phase 3 lowers purinergic danger signaling, restores organ function, and returns the body to the Health Cycle . According to the essay, epidemiological estimates cited around this work note tens of millions of COVID survivors experiencing ME/CFS-like syndromes or chronic disability, with 10–30% struggling to recover under conventional care. 28.body: To exit a stalled Cell Danger Response without relying solely on scarce pharmaceuticals, Dr. Robert K. Naviaux advocates salugenesis : actively cultivating the signals of health so the brain and autonomic nervous system broadcast safety to defensive tissues (see The Six Cardinal Elements ). "Healing is an active process that requires positive reinforcement with non-danger, safety and security signals from the brain... If long-distance safety signals are not re-established after the initial damage from infection or injury are repaired, the tissue defaults to chronic defense at the cellular level." — Dr. Robert K. Naviaux , quoted in Systemic Treatments for the Cell Danger Response Drawing on Naviaux's model and decades of clinical observations, the essay emphasizes four practical pillars for rebooting the Healing Cycle:

29.body: Sympathetic vs. parasympathetic balance: Excitatory sympathetic circuits (fight-or-flight, vigilance, anxiety) sustain the CDR, while inhibitory parasympathetic circuits broadcast calming safety signals. Chronically ill CDR patients typically live locked in sympathetic over-activation and parasympathetic deficiency . The vagus nerve ("the great wanderer and protector"): Branching throughout the body's organs, the vagus nerve is studded with ATP receptors that monitor tissues for active cellular danger and relay alerts back to the brain—and in reverse, delivers whole-body safety signals down to organs when CDR3 is ready to close.
29.breadcrumbs: Rebooting the Healing Cycle (Salugenesis) » 1. Autonomic Balance & The Vagus Nerve
29.title: 1. Autonomic Balance & The Vagus Nerve

30.body: Deep delta-wave sleep: During restorative deep sleep, slow delta waves help the nervous system transmit body-wide safety signals. Active CDR signaling routinely fractures sleep, creating a vicious circle. Why common sleep drugs backfire: The author stresses that conventional "sleep" medications are largely neurological sedatives that knock out consciousness while suppressing the restorative sleep phases needed for healing. Adenosine & caffeine: As normal daytime metabolism breaks down ATP, adenosine accumulates and promotes sleep pressure—while also directly counteracting aspects of the CDR . Caffeine stays stimulatory for hours by blocking brain adenosine receptors, which can interfere with insomnia recovery. The author notes curiosity about a favorite traditional herb for pain and insomnia that acts on adenosine receptors.
30.breadcrumbs: Rebooting the Healing Cycle (Salugenesis) » 2. Restorative Sleep Architecture & Adenosine
30.title: 2. Restorative Sleep Architecture & Adenosine

31.body: Beyond avoiding blue light at night to protect circadian melatonin/sleep timing, the essay reports mentors' consensus that modern technology has severed multiple ancient biological rhythms over the last 150 years: Thermal contrast: Warmth during active daylight hours, coolness at night. Activity alternation: Cycling between deliberate movement and genuine physical rest. Cognitive pacing: Avoiding continuous unbroken nervous-system demand (citing the heuristic of resting after roughly seven sequential decisions—nearly impossible during nonstop screen/computer work). Cases where patients temporarily adopted off-grid primitive routines (e.g., living through winter with a wood stove and no electricity) were cited as illustrating dramatic health improvements once daily life forced alignment with natural environmental cycles.
31.breadcrumbs: Rebooting the Healing Cycle (Salugenesis) » 3. Natural & Circadian Biological Rhythms
31.title: 3. Natural & Circadian Biological Rhythms

32.body: A critical principle highlighted from Naviaux's work: biological regulation responds to pulsed signals, not constant flooding . Why continuous "good things" reverse benefit: Integrative practitioners frequently take a beneficial stimulus or supplement and administer it nonstop, blunting or reversing the adaptive response. Consolidation takes ~3 months: Even after initial improvement, newly re-established Health Cycle signaling remains fragile and needs protected, low-stress intervals spanning roughly three months (one full season) to lock in. Unresolved early trauma & toxins: Without an active salugenic reset, lingering danger memories from childhood trauma or past toxic exposures can keep patches of tissue parked in low-grade cellular defense for decades until later stress tips them into overt chronic disease. 33.body: To understand why chronic CDR states spread across tissues and resist ordinary interventions, Naviaux's model focuses on purinergic danger signaling .
33.breadcrumbs: Extracellular ATP, Purinergic Signaling & Mast Cells » Extracellular ATP, Purinergic Signaling & Mast Cells
33.title: Extracellular ATP, Purinergic Signaling & Mast Cells

34.body: Inside a healthy cell, ATP (adenosine triphosphate) concentration is roughly one million times higher than outside the cell. Because of that steep gradient: When a cell is physically damaged or stressed, ATP and related purine molecules escape into the extracellular space—both passively from injury and actively through membrane channels (such as pannexin channels) that open when danger is sensed. Surrounding cells and nerves detect that leaked ATP via specialized surface sensors called purinergic receptors (19 receptors identified across the body). This turns extracellular ATP into an evolutionarily conserved "smoke alarm": "a neighbor is in trouble—seal down and enter the CDR." Intracellular ATP (~1,000,000x higher) │ ├──> Cell membrane channels open / cell damage ▼ Extracellular ATP & purines leak out │ ├──> Binds purinergic receptors (19 subtypes) on neighbors, nerves & mast cells └──> Sustains CDR loop, hypersensitivity & mast cell degranulation
34.breadcrumbs: Extracellular ATP, Purinergic Signaling & Mast Cells » Extracellular ATP: The Universal Danger Alarm
34.title: Extracellular ATP: The Universal Danger Alarm

35.body: If persistent purinergic signaling keeps cells trapped in the CDR, antipurinergic drugs (APDs) aim to block those receptors so tissues can receive safety signals again: Suramin (broad-spectrum blocker): Developed a century ago for African sleeping sickness, suramin is currently the only drug tested in humans that broadly inhibits all purinergic receptor subtypes. (See Antipurinergic Therapy, Suramin & ISR for clinical trial outcomes and availability.) Targeted experimental blockers cited in the essay: Brilliant Blue G: Reported improvement in animal models of Parkinson's disease and acetaminophen-induced liver injury. Suramin in acute liver models: Protected against Fas-induced acute fulminant hepatitis in mouse studies. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD): A targeted APD reduced gut inflammation in mice and improved response to conventional therapy. P2X7 receptor inhibitors: Multiple targeted drugs targeting the P2X7 purinergic receptor have entered clinical trials for rheumatoid arthritis and pain .
35.breadcrumbs: Extracellular ATP, Purinergic Signaling & Mast Cells » Antipurinergic Therapy (APT) & Experimental Receptor Blockers
35.title: Antipurinergic Therapy (APT) & Experimental Receptor Blockers

36.body: Purinergic ATP signaling directly amplifies pain and heat sensory perception . That overlap explains two common patterns in complex chronic illnesses: Calming the CDR frequently relieves stubborn chronic pain alongside systemic fatigue. Patients develop dramatic hypersensitivity to light, sound, heat, medications, or minor physical triggers. (Note: A Midwestern Doctor adds an alternative vascular hypothesis alongside purinergic sensitization—suggesting some chronic hypersensitivity may reflect collapsed zeta potential causing microstrokes in the thalamus , the brain region responsible for gating pain signals.)

36.title: Chronic Pain & Sensory Hypersensitivity

37.body: One of the essay's most clinically relevant connections is between purinergic signaling and mast cells , immune sentinels that release histamine during inflammatory defense ( CDR1 ): Extracellular ATP, ADP, adenosine, and UDP-glucose act as core regulators triggering mast cell degranulation . A 2019 study cited in the essay demonstrated that blocking purinergic receptors with suramin suppresses mast cell degranulation . In complex chronic conditions—and notably in post-COVID and vaccine-injury cohorts discussed by the author—mast cells become hair-trigger sensitive, degranulating in response to mild foods, scents, temperature shifts, or everyday stressors. 39.body: Conventional medicine treats autism as largely untreatable, yet several biological clues point toward ongoing metabolic signaling regulation: Core autism symptoms frequently improve transiently during fevers (recall that fevers arise in acute inflammatory CDR1 , whereas autism reflects a non-fever CDR3 connectivity/differentiation block). Shared genetic variants linked to increased ASD risk commonly participate in CDR signaling or maintenance .

41.body: In autism mouse models—even when treatment was delayed until the human biological age-equivalent of 30 years old —antipurinergic therapy with suramin completely corrected core behavioral and metabolic abnormalities. However, gait deficits tied to permanent structural loss of cerebellar Purkinje cells did not reverse, illustrating the boundary between functional signaling lock-in and structural cell loss .
41.breadcrumbs: Antipurinergic Therapy, Suramin & ISR » 1. Adult Mouse Reversal Studies
41.title: 1. Adult Mouse Reversal Studies

42.body: Design: 10 boys aged 5–14; 5 received a single low-dose intravenous infusion of suramin (5–15 μM blood target); 5 received placebo. Outcomes: All 5 boys on suramin improved across core ASD domains (language, social interaction, restricted interests, repetitive behaviors) for 5–8 weeks , while none of the placebo group showed those gains. Two previously non-verbal boys spoke their first sentences. Therapy synergy: Blocking the CDR dramatically amplified responsiveness to regular school, speech therapy, occupational therapy, educational enrichment, and applied behavioral analysis (ABA). Safety: Blood monitoring showed only a mild, transient, asymptomatic macular rash covering 1–20% of skin (~1 day post-infusion, fading naturally in 2–4 days).
42.breadcrumbs: Antipurinergic Therapy, Suramin & ISR » 2. Naviaux's 2017 Pilot Clinical Trial
42.title: 2. Naviaux's 2017 Pilot Clinical Trial

43.body: Design: Founded in 2018 to commercialize Naviaux's approach, PaxMedica ran a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 52 boys with moderate-to-severe autism using IV suramin at week 0, week 4, and week 8 (final evaluation 6 weeks after the third infusion). Outcomes & status: Conference presentations (and direct sources cited by the author) reported significant clinical benefit over placebo, though a peer-reviewed journal publication and larger follow-up trial remained pending at the time of writing. Observed adverse events: Mostly mild-to-moderate rash, upper respiratory infection, and vomiting resolving without intervention (plus one serious adverse event in a participant with multiple comorbidities that resolved without sequelae after acute treatment).
43.breadcrumbs: Antipurinergic Therapy, Suramin & ISR » 3. PaxMedica South Africa Trial (52 Boys)
43.title: 3. PaxMedica South Africa Trial (52 Boys)

44.body: Long half-life: Earlier studies established a suramin half-life of 14.7 ± 0.7 days in ~90% of subjects (10% clear it faster)—matching the 5–8 week benefit window from one dose. Dividing a monthly infusion into five weekly infusions extended its half-life 3–4× in earlier African research. Why patients cannot get it: Bayer shut down the sole global manufacturing plant for commercial reasons tied to declining sleeping-sickness economics. Because that parasite does not exist in the United States, suramin has no FDA approval and cannot legally be imported for human clinical use without regulatory clearance. PaxMedica has sought capital to build a new manufacturing line. Botanical leads: The essay notes peer-reviewed studies identifying antipurinergic properties in certain natural herbs , whose known traditional effects align with blocking purinergic danger signaling.

44.title: Pharmacology & The Availability Bottleneck

45.body: Another line of research parallel to the CDR targets age-related cognitive decline via the Integrated Stress Response (ISR) : "With age there is a marked decline of protein synthesis in the brain that correlates with defects in proper protein folding. Accumulation of misfolded proteins can activate the integrated stress response (ISR), an evolutionary conserved pathway that decreases protein synthesis." — Quoted in Systemic Treatments for the Cell Danger Response Experimental ISR inhibitors restored neuronal structure, brain cell function, and memory performance in aging models. (Author hypothesis) : A Midwestern Doctor speculates that remdesivir (an RNA-polymerase inhibitor) could partially suppress human protein synthesis or coincide with a systemic CDR, noting post-hospitalization COVID patients whose prolotherapy tissue-repair treatments failed to trigger healing for months afterward. 48.body: Aside from suramin (which remains unavailable and only suppresses the CDR for roughly two weeks unless the root driver is gone), there is no single systemic switch that moves every cell cleanly through CDR1 → CDR2 → CDR3 → normal. Because different tissues across the body sit in different CDR states at the same time , practitioners need to specify which cells or organ system they are trying to move back into normal function. Just as valuable: the CDR identifies which therapies to avoid and which abnormal markers represent protective compensations to respect rather than forcibly override.
48.breadcrumbs: Working with the CDR in Clinical Practice » 1. A Diagnostic Map, Not a Single "Magic Bullet"
48.title: 1. A Diagnostic Map, Not a Single "Magic Bullet"

49.body: Cells trapped in a longstanding CDR often become progressively hypersensitive to any sudden physiological shift—even therapies meant to cleanse, nourish, or stimulate repair. Paradoxically, even a careful low-dose intervention aimed at advancing healing can signal the nervous system to snap back into danger defense. This creates difficult timing dilemmas: Attacking a lingering infection (e.g., Lyme) aggressively while the patient is locked in feedback loops often explodes CDR inflammation. Past dangers long resolved (years earlier) vs. currently ongoing triggers require opposite starting sequences. (Author note: the author suggests this distinguishes post-COVID syndromes that resolve after one intervention from mRNA spike-protein injuries where persistent antigen requires repeated treatment.)

50.body: When a CDR coexists with an active trigger or toxic load, clinicians typically follow one of three sequences: Path A (Danger already gone): Treat CDR ──> Rebuild Health Cycle Path B (Ongoing threat dominates): Clear active danger ──> Treat CDR Path C (Reactive feedback loops): Calm CDR ──> Clear active danger ──> Calm CDR again

51.body: Before moving pathogens or forcing shifts, the clinician often has to address: Fluid circulation & zeta potential: Stagnant microcirculation acts as a primary CDR trigger by itself—and when toxins or die-off are mobilized without draining pathways, localized buildup triggers severe flares (e.g., why starting antibiotics abruptly in a Lyme patient with poor circulation frequently backfires). Gentle "pretox" before detox: Lightly preparing elimination pathways before deeper detoxification so mobilized burdens don't re-alarm hypersensitive cells. Track durable state change vs. temporary dampening: Always verify whether an intervention merely muted symptoms for days or actually shifted the tissue into stable health.

52.body: Both the clinician and Dr. Robert K. Naviaux stress that anti-CDR interventions are temporary bridges , not lifelong crutches: "Antipurinergic drugs like suramin, pannexin 1 (PANX1) channel blockers, and other salugenesis therapies are part of induction therapy to reboot healing. They are not meant to be taken for life. These interventions are meant to be bridges. During the induction phase, interventions are meant to act like a cast for a broken leg—they are intended to support the healing process and protect injured tissues from further damage. Once the healing cycle is completed and reentry into the health cycle occurs, then antipurinergic therapy can be discontinued." — Dr. Robert K. Naviaux , quoted in Systemic Treatments for the Cell Danger Response Next: Hormone Resistance, Fasting & Ketogenic Metabolism · Related: Cultivating Health vs. Disease-Centered Medicine · Rebooting Salugenesis

53.body: When cells enter the Cell Danger Response , they intentionally downregulate metabolism and decouple from outside instructions—creating counterintuitive reactions to hormones, mitochondrial supplements, fasting, and diet.
53.breadcrumbs: Hormone Resistance, Fasting & Ketogenic Metabolism » Hormone Resistance, Fasting & Ketogenic Metabolism
53.title: Hormone Resistance, Fasting & Ketogenic Metabolism

54.body: In chronic CDR conditions, a patient rarely has 100% healthy or 100% trapped tissue—most organs contain a mosaic of normal responsive cells alongside unresponsive CDR-locked cells. This creates two major clinical traps: Pushing hormones (thyroid, insulin, growth factors): Unresponsive CDR cells ignore standard signaling, while neighboring responsive cells get over-stimulated , producing dependency (as seen with escalating insulin) and iatrogenic side effects—while trying to force dormant cells awake before they are ready destabilizes healing. Pushing mitochondrial supplements: Because mitochondria deliberately dial down energy output as an adaptive survival shield, trying to brute-force mitochondrial throughput without clearing the CDR can over-activate healthy cells or provoke inflammatory backlash.
54.breadcrumbs: Hormone Resistance, Fasting & Ketogenic Metabolism » 1. End-Organ Hormone & Mitochondrial Resistance
54.title: 1. End-Organ Hormone & Mitochondrial Resistance

55.body: Naviaux on "exhaustion" syndromes: Apparent thyroid or adrenal failure in chronic illness often fails classical deficiency criteria; glands retain residual capacity under physiologic stimulation, but output and tissue sensitivity are adaptively suppressed . (Author clinical note) : Some colleagues report monitoring reverse T3 alongside standard thyroid panels and testing low doses of T3 (Cytomel) —written as "in the range of 2.5 mg" in the original Substack text—rather than conventional T4 (Synthroid) regimens when tissue signaling resistance is present.

56.body: Why fasting helps: Both intermittent and extended fasting lower excessive immune reactivity and dampen inflammatory signaling. Fasting also induces autophagy , encouraging the body to dismantle severely dysfunctional, CDR-trapped cells that disrupt neighboring healthy tissue. Its limit: While helpful for symptom load, fasting by itself typically cannot clear every trapped cell cluster or reboot a deeply locked systemic CDR on its own.

59.body: Debates over whether ketogenic diets are universally healthy miss how CDR metabolism changes fuel preference : A recent animal study cited in the essay injected ATP into mice to trigger the CDR and observed cells switching rapidly from balanced carbohydrate oxidation to near-complete dependence on fatty acids . What this explains: Conditions characterized by trapped central-nervous-system CDR (such as epilepsy ) often respond dramatically to ketogenic diets because ketones and fatty acids feed cells locked in that altered fuel state. The caveat: At the same time, it implies pure fatty-acid dependence reflects a defensive survival mode , rather than necessarily representing the ideal fuel mix for healthy, un-stressed tissue. 60.body: In the final public sections of the essay, A Midwestern Doctor links the Cell Danger Response directly to regenerative medicine —explaining why damaged or aging tissues stop performing and what is required to bring dormant cells back online.

60.title: Dormant Tissue, Scars, Aging & Neurodegeneration

61.body: Regenerative therapies restore lost organ function through two pathways: Cell replacement: Replacing permanently lost tissue with new cells (e.g., via stem-cell recruitment). Reactivating dormant tissue: Waking up living cells that have entered non-functional, non-dividing survival dormancy. Because dormancy turns out to be far more common than outright cell destruction—and because the CDR itself drives cells into dormant low-output states—methods built to wake dormant tissue become prime candidates for resolving stubborn CDRs.
61.breadcrumbs: Dormant Tissue, Scars, Aging & Neurodegeneration » Regenerative Medicine's Two Modes
61.title: Regenerative Medicine's Two Modes

62.body: Sometimes chronic systemic trouble starts in a localized patch of trapped cells: Surgical scars as CDR foci: Incomplete healing along surgical incision lines can leave scar tissue parked in chronic CDR activation. Beyond local discomfort, persistent danger signaling from a scar can irritate the central nervous system and generate distant systemic symptoms that sometimes clear rapidly after treating the scar directly (e.g., via neural therapy ). Cumulative sensitization: Cells stuck in the CDR become primed to overreact to new threats. (Author observation) : Following persistent spike-protein exposure from mRNA vaccination, old previously silent scars sometimes flared with intense pain and improved once treated locally. When the danger triggers cells throughout the entire body, however, local injections aren't enough—requiring a systemic approach.
62.breadcrumbs: Dormant Tissue, Scars, Aging & Neurodegeneration » Local Scars, Neural Therapy & Amplification
62.title: Local Scars, Neural Therapy & Amplification

63.body: Drawing on an earlier series, A Midwestern Doctor argues that conventional Alzheimer's research wrongly attacks downstream protective adaptations while ignoring viable non-commercial treatments, framing the condition as brain cells shutting down into dormancy and later getting pruned away during brain remodeling. In that framework, reversing neuronal loss requires three coordinated steps: Remove ongoing cellular shocks causing dormancy — Identifying toxic drivers, especially highlighting inhaled surgical anesthetics used to temporarily silence neurons during operations alongside other neurotoxins. Sustain cellular nourishment — Supplying nutritional substrates, active cognitive stimulation, and restoring cerebral circulation . Help neurons exit dormancy — Mitigating brain CDR signaling; examples mentioned in the essay include: Subcutaneous aluminum-free B1 and B12 support (especially before and after surgery) to sustain the Krebs cycle. DMSO (noted by the author as a favored tool for reviving CDR-impaired neurological cells, such as after stroke).

63.title: Alzheimer's Disease Framed as Neuronal Dormancy

64.body: Hair follicles cycle cleanly through three observable phases: Anagen: Active growth phase Catagen: Pruning/transition phase Telogen: Dormant resting phase When stress pushes follicles to linger too long in telogen ( Telogen Effluvium ), visible thinning occurs. The essay points out that effective regenerative therapies for hair loss weren't invented specifically for hair—they work because they shift cells out of resting dormancy (telogen) and back into active growth (anagen) .

73.body: Term Meaning in This Framework Antipurinergic Drugs (APDs) Compounds that block purinergic ATP danger receptors (e.g., suramin, Brilliant Blue G, P2X7 inhibitors) to quiet chronic CDR loops Cell Danger Response (CDR) Conserved mitochondrial defense shift that prioritizes cell survival over normal organ work and signals nearby tissues to brace for threat CDR1 Phase 1 (inflammatory): cells seal off and neutralize microbial/toxic threats; chronic lock-in drives inflammatory conditions CDR2 Phase 2 (proliferative): replaces biomass, vessels, and stem cells; chronic lock-in drives proliferative disorders including cancer CDR3 Phase 3 (reintegration & differentiation): inflammation resolves and cells reconnect with nerves/hormones; chronic lock-in drives neurodevelopmental, psychiatric, and neurodegenerative conditions Functional Reserve Capacity Whole-organism resilience built over weeks/months when the Six Cardinal Elements of the Health Cycle are consistently present Health Cycle Normal energetic, communicative, restorative daily physiology governed by Naviaux's six cardinal elements Healing Cycle Naviaux's updated name for the full CDR1 → CDR2 → CDR3 repair arc when it successfully completes and exits Hypometabolic Survival State Low-energy cellular hibernation shunt seen in ME/CFS, long-COVID, and chronic Lyme where mitochondria stall between normal work and full repair Induction Therapy Temporary "cast for a broken leg" interventions used only until the Healing Cycle completes and the body re-enters the Health Cycle Integrated Stress Response (ISR) Conserved protein-synthesis-dampening pathway activated by misfolded proteins/stress that overlaps CDR biology in age-related cognitive decline Mast Cell Activation Hypersensitive immune degranulation (histamine release in CDR1) regulated by extracellular purines like ATP, ADP, adenosine, and UDP-glucose Pluricausal Disease Chronic illness arising from cumulative deficits across multiple health generators and combined low-grade stressors rather than one single pathogen or lesion Pretox Gentle pre-conditioning of elimination and circulation pathways prior to active detoxification so hypersensitive CDR patients don't crash Purinergic Signaling Danger-warning network driven by extracellular ATP (~1,000,000× higher inside cells than outside) binding 19 cell-surface purine receptors Salugenesis Active creation of health via safety signals (vagal tone, deep sleep, natural rhythms, and the six cardinal elements) to terminate chronic defense Suramin Century-old sleeping sickness drug and broad-spectrum purinergic receptor blocker tested in Naviaux's low-dose autism pilot and PaxMedica's follow-up RCT Telogen Effluvium Hair thinning from follicles remaining stuck in the resting (telogen) phase instead of re-entering active growth (anagen) Zeta Potential Electrical repulsion stability keeping suspended particles/cells dispersed in biological fluids; cited by the author as important for microcirculation and toxin drainage Source: Systemic Treatments for the Cell Danger Response (Substack) · Back to: Overview
